problem: The trap reads 'Do not evaluate on training patches or train only on high-resolution targets.' Read literally, this tells students not to train on high-resolution targets — but the high-resolution image is exactly the supervision in super-resolution training. The real pitfall it is reaching for is a mismatch between the low-resolution images used in training and those seen at test time.
fix: Super-resolution input is low-resolution. Evaluate on held-out low/high-resolution pairs, not on training patches, and build the low-resolution training inputs with the same downscaling (degradation) you will meet at test time.

where: Section 2, the probability expression p(y | x ⊙ (1 − m), m)
problem: The symbol y is never defined, and the mask polarity only becomes clear from the surrounding text, so a student reading the formula alone cannot tell what y or m are.
fix: Write: p(y | x ⊙ (1 − m), m), where y is the full target image, x is the observed image, m is a binary mask with m = 1 at missing pixels, and ⊙ is the elementwise product.

problem: The sentence about 3D object generation from voxels or point clouds is a different application and interrupts the super-resolution evaluation point.
fix: Delete the clause about 3D object generation (or move it to a later chapter on 3D generation); keep the CCTV restoration remark, which is an image task.

problem: 'PSNR is not “higher is always better” perceptually' is tangled and can be misread as saying higher PSNR is worse. The intended meaning is that a higher PSNR does not guarantee a better-looking image.
fix: Higher PSNR does not always mean a better-looking image; PSNR rewards smooth blur. Report SSIM or a perceptual metric as well.

problem: 'it ranges up to 1 for identical images' gives no lower bound, so students cannot say what the scale is.
fix: 'it takes values up to 1 (typically between 0 and 1), and equals 1 for identical images'.
